Bug: notification titles and meal plan notifications are always in English.

Notifications sent through the event bus (Apprise and the other listeners) get their title from EventBusMessage.from_type, which turns the event type's name into English (EventTypes.mealplan_entry_created becomes "Mealplan Entry Created"). Meal plan entries also send a hard-coded English body naming the date and the raw entry type value. Users who run Mealie in another language still get English, and "Mealplan" is not even a word.

Expected:
1. EventBusMessage.from_type(event_type, body="", translator=None) takes a new optional keyword argument translator, after body; EventBusMessage and EventTypes stay where they are. A translator is anything with t(key, default=None, **kwargs), such as a JsonProvider (mealie.pkgs.i18n.json_provider) or what get_locale_provider returns.
   - With a translator, the title is its translation of notifications.event-title.<name>, where <name> is the EventTypes member name with underscores replaced by hyphens (mealplan_entry_created uses notifications.event-title.mealplan-entry-created). Example: with a JsonProvider built from a dict in which notifications > event-title > mealplan-entry-created is "已创建膳食计划条目", and body "测试正文", the title is "已创建膳食计划条目" and the body stays "测试正文".
   - If the translator has no such key, the title falls back to today's English title, never the key itself: with JsonProvider({}) it is "Mealplan Entry Created".
   - Without a translator nothing changes: title "Mealplan Entry Created", the body as given, and an empty body still becomes "generic".
2. The backend's en-US translation catalogue (the one get_locale_provider serves for en-US, which already holds notifications.generic-created and mealplan.no-recipes-match-your-rules) gains:
   - a notifications.event-title.<name> entry for every one of the 27 EventTypes members, from test-message and webhook-task through label-deleted, none missing. The English titles are the member names in title case, except that the three meal plan titles read "Meal Plan Entry Created", "Meal Plan Entry Updated" and "Meal Plan Entry Deleted". So from_type(EventTypes.mealplan_entry_created, translator=JsonProvider(<that catalogue>)) gives the title "Meal Plan Entry Created".
   - mealplan.entry-type.<type> for each meal plan entry type (breakfast, lunch, dinner, side, snack, drink, dessert), each the lower-case English word (mealplan.entry-type.dinner is "dinner").
   - notifications.mealplan-entry-created, notifications.mealplan-entry-updated and notifications.mealplan-entry-deleted, with the placeholders {date} and {entry_type}. Translating notifications.mealplan-entry-created with date "2026-08-17" and entry_type set to the translation of mealplan.entry-type.dinner gives exactly "Meal plan entry created for 2026-08-17 for dinner"; the updated and deleted messages read the same with "updated" and "deleted".
   - a body for the test notification.
3. Events raised while handling a request use that request's language (Accept-Language): meal plan entry notifications (POST /api/households/mealplans, POST /api/households/mealplans/random, PUT and DELETE /api/households/mealplans/{item_id}) get the translated title and the translated body above, with the translated entry type (the raw value when there is no translation), and the test notification (POST /api/households/events/notifications/{item_id}/test) gets a translated title and body. Events raised outside a request, such as by scheduled tasks, keep the English title.

fix-ec3e0305.text:
Bug: recipes still expose a group-wide "last made" date that mixes households.

Last-made dates are tracked per household. PATCH /api/recipes/{slug}/last-made records the time for the caller's household, and GET /api/households/self/recipes/{slug} returns it as lastMade. But each recipe also still carries a group-wide lastMade, the latest date any household made it. This value is updated in the background whenever a household's date changes, and also by the meal-plan timeline task. It appears as lastMade in recipe JSON (GET /api/recipes/{slug}, recipe lists, suggestions and the public explore pages), so users see another household's activity as if it were theirs. Anonymous visitors of a public group can also sort and filter recipes by it.

Expected:

1. The recipe schemas Recipe and RecipeSummary no longer have a last_made field, so recipe JSON (a single recipe, lists, suggestions and the explore endpoints) has no lastMade key at all. HouseholdRecipeSummary (in mealie.schema.household.household) keeps last_made, and it becomes the only place where the value is exposed.

2. Nothing writes the group-wide value any more. Keep the recipes.last_made column and the RecipeModel.last_made attribute: household-aware lastMade filtering and sorting, and cookbook filter validation, are built on them, and the column may be read directly. Leave its value NULL, with no database migration. For example, after anyone calls PATCH /api/recipes/{slug}/last-made, selecting RecipeModel.last_made for that recipe from the database gives None. The same holds after the meal-plan timeline task (create_mealplan_timeline_events) runs.

3. Per-household behaviour stays as it is:
   - PATCH /api/recipes/{slug}/last-made stays in the API and answers 200 for any user of the group, including on another household's recipe, whether or not that household is private or locks recipe edits, and on locked recipes.
   - It sets the caller's household's lastMade to exactly the given timestamp, even when that is earlier than the stored one. A UTC ISO timestamp sent with a "Z" suffix is returned as the same string by GET /api/households/self/recipes/{slug}.
   - Other households are not affected, and their lastMade stays null.
   - The meal-plan timeline task still creates the event and sets the household's lastMade to today. It changes nothing else on the recipe apart from dateUpdated and updatedAt.

4. Recipe queries made for a signed-in user (a recipes repository bound with by_user, as GET /api/recipes is) keep supporting lastMade in orderBy and queryFilter. As today, it is resolved against that user's household. Cookbooks can still be saved with a lastMade filter.

5. The public explore endpoints have no household, so they must refuse lastMade instead of using a stale value:
   - GET /api/explore/groups/{group_slug}/recipes and GET /api/explore/groups/{group_slug}/recipes/suggestions answer 400 when orderBy names lastMade (or last_made, also inside a comma-separated list or with a :asc/:desc suffix).
   - They also answer 400 when queryFilter has a condition on lastMade, e.g. "lastMade IS NOT NULL".
   - The same applies to the filter of a public cookbook selected with ?cookbook=<id>: a public cookbook in a public household whose filter is "lastMade IS NOT NULL" gives 400.
   - Only conditions on the attribute count. queryFilter 'name = "last_made"' still answers 200, and an invalid filter such as 'name IS "last_made"' still answers 400, as any invalid filter does.
   - All other public queries behave as before.

6. CopyMeThat import: the export marks some recipes as made ("I made this", the made_this element). The importer used to put that on the group-wide value. Instead, it now records the import time as the importing user's household's last-made date for those recipes. After importing tests/data/migrations/copymethat.zip, GET /api/households/self/recipes/spam-zoodles with the importer's token answers 200 with a non-empty lastMade, and every report entry is still a success.

UI changes are not part of this task.

Security report: server-initiated HTTP requests can be aimed at internal addresses (SSRF and DNS rebinding).

Mealie sends HTTP requests to URLs that users control: recipe and image scraping, household webhooks, "post" recipe actions, and the OIDC picture claim. The guards are incomplete:
- Webhooks (WebhookPublisher.publish) and post-type recipe actions (POST /api/households/recipe-actions/{item_id}/trigger/{recipe_slug}) send with a plain requests.post, so any household member can make the server POST to 127.0.0.1, a LAN service or the cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254.
- The scraper's AsyncSafeTransport resolves the host once, checks that single address with is_private only, and then lets curl resolve the name again when it connects, so a rebinding DNS answer can swap in an internal address. It also lets through carrier-grade NAT (100.64.0.0/10), IPv4-mapped IPv6 such as ::ffff:127.0.0.1, multicast and unspecified addresses, and an unresolvable host escapes as a raw socket error.
- The OIDC avatar download checks the addresses itself and then connects separately, with the same race.
- Operators can neither allow a known internal server nor block a public host.

Expected:

1. Settings. AppSettings (what get_app_settings returns) gets HTTP_ALLOW_LIST and HTTP_DISALLOW_LIST, both read from the environment with default "", each a comma-separated list of host names, IP addresses or CIDRs, exposed as the list properties http_allow_list and http_disallow_list (entries trimmed, empty ones dropped). Allowed entries may be reached even when they resolve to an otherwise blocked address. Disallowed entries are never reached, even when public, and they win over the allow list.

2. Address policy. A new function is_blocked_ip(ip) in the safehttp transport module (the one that defines AsyncSafeTransport and InvalidDomainError), also exported by the safehttp package. It takes an ipaddress.IPv4Address or IPv6Address and returns True for addresses that are never reachable by default: private, loopback, link-local, multicast, reserved, unspecified, and 100.64.0.0/10. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address is judged by the IPv4 address inside it. It returns False for 8.8.8.8 and 2606:4700:4700::1111, and True for 10.0.0.1, 172.16.5.5, 192.168.1.1, 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254, 100.64.0.1, 0.0.0.0, 224.0.0.1, ::1, fe80::1, fc00::1 and ::ffff:127.0.0.1.

3. Transports. Next to AsyncSafeTransport (still built on httpx-curl-cffi's AsyncCurlTransport and still handling requests in handle_async_request), add a sync SafeTransport in the same module: a subclass of httpx-curl-cffi's CurlTransport, which that module imports under the name CurlTransport. Both take the keyword-only options log, allow_hosts and deny_hosts (sequences of host names, IPs or CIDRs, empty by default) and timeout (15 by default, forced onto every request as today), and pass every other keyword (impersonate, default_headers, verify, proxy and so on) to the curl transport. AsyncSafeTransport() and SafeTransport() work without arguments.
   Every request, and so every redirect hop, is checked by a plain (not async) method _validate(request) before anything connects:
   - An IP-literal host is checked as it is. A host name is resolved with socket.getaddrinfo(host, port, ...) and every distinct address it returns is checked; the port is the URL's, else 443 for https and 80 for http. If resolution fails (socket.gaierror, or UnicodeError for a name that cannot be encoded) it raises InvalidDomainError.
   - The deny list comes first: if the host name equals a deny entry (ignoring case) or any address falls inside a deny network, it raises InvalidDomainError even when the host is also on the allow list. "blocked.example" on both lists is blocked, and deny "93.184.216.0/24" blocks a public host resolving to 93.184.216.34.
   - Unless the target is allowed (its host name equals an allow entry, or an address falls inside an allow network), any blocked address among those resolved raises InvalidDomainError: one public address plus 127.0.0.1 is rejected, and so is a name resolving to ::1 or to 10.0.0.5. Allow "internal.example" lets internal.example reach 10.0.0.5, and allow "10.0.0.0/8" lets a name resolving to 10.1.2.3 through.
   - It returns None for an IP-literal host (https://93.184.216.34/ passes and returns None; http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ raises InvalidDomainError). Otherwise it returns curl RESOLVE entries of the form "host:port:address", one per address in resolver order: https://example.test/path resolving to 93.184.216.34 gives ["example.test:443:93.184.216.34"]; http://example.test/ resolving to 93.184.216.34 and 93.184.216.35 gives ["example.test:80:93.184.216.34", "example.test:80:93.184.216.35"]; the allowed cases give ["internal.example:443:10.0.0.5"] and ["internal.example:443:10.1.2.3"].
   _apply_pin(entries) stores such a list as CurlOpt.RESOLVE in the curl session's options (transport._session.curl_options), or removes CurlOpt.RESOLVE when given None, and leaves the other options alone. Each request is validated, pinned and only then handed to the curl base class, so the connection goes to exactly the checked addresses: an AsyncSafeTransport with allow_hosts=["pinned.example"], under a resolver that answers 127.0.0.1, really reaches a local server at http://pinned.example:<port>/ (200, body "OK"). A rejected request never reaches the base class's handle_request or handle_async_request.
   Proxies: with no proxy argument, transport._session.curl_options[CurlOpt.NOPROXY] is "*", so ambient HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY variables cannot send the request through a proxy that would resolve the name itself; with proxy="http://proxy:8080" it is "" (the explicit proxy applies to every host), and applying a pin leaves it "". With a configured proxy the pin cannot hold, since the proxy resolves names; that trade-off is the operator's.

4. post(url, *, json=None, timeout=15, allow_hosts=(), deny_hosts=(), **kwargs), a module-level function in the transport module, exported by the safehttp package as safehttp.post. It sends a sync POST through SafeTransport with httpx, follows redirects (each hop checked again) and returns the httpx.Response; InvalidDomainError reaches the caller unchanged. A POST to http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ raises InvalidDomainError by default and succeeds (status 200) with allow_hosts=["127.0.0.1"].

5. Webhooks and recipe actions send through safehttp.post with allow_hosts and deny_hosts taken from http_allow_list and http_disallow_list. They look post up on the safehttp package each time they send, so replacing the package's post attribute (as a monkeypatch does) intercepts every outbound POST. A webhook passes the URL as the first positional argument, the event payload as json= and timeout=15. The recipe-action trigger still answers 202 for a post action, 404 for an unknown action or recipe, and 400 for a link action. Recipe-action CRUD with its URL rule (only http and https, in any case, otherwise 422) and webhook CRUD are unchanged.

6. Scraping. _build_transport(impersonate, proxy=None), in the module that holds resilient_fetch, still builds AsyncSafeTransport with keyword arguments only and now adds allow_hosts=http_allow_list and deny_hosts=http_disallow_list, from get_app_settings() called inside _build_transport each time it runs. It passes a proxy keyword only when a proxy is given. Nothing else in the fetch loop reads the two lists, and resilient_fetch otherwise behaves as today (challenge detection, impersonation rotation, backoff, proxy modes, FlareSolverr).

7. OIDC avatar (OpenIDProvider and the picture claim):
   - As today, no request is made when the claim is missing, not a string or empty (None, 123, a dict, ""), when it still points at the stored image (the sha256 hex of the URL equals external_avatar_hash), when it cannot be parsed ("https://[::1", or a host with a 300-character label), or when it is not https: http://cdn.example.com/a.png, file:///etc/passwd, ftp://cdn.example.com/a.png and not-a-url are never requested. The provider's own host (the host of OIDC_CONFIGURATION_URL) may use http or https.
   - The download goes through SafeTransport, so its network I/O happens in CurlTransport.handle_request and its DNS lookups in socket.getaddrinfo. Its allow list is HTTP_ALLOW_LIST plus the provider's own host; its deny list is HTTP_DISALLOW_LIST, which wins even over the provider's host. A picture host resolving to 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.5, 192.168.1.10, 169.254.169.254, 100.64.0.1, ::1, fd00::1 or ::ffff:127.0.0.1 is never requested, nor is an unresolvable one, nor a public cdn.example.com when HTTP_DISALLOW_LIST=cdn.example.com. The provider's host idp.example.com resolving to 192.168.1.10 is fetched with exactly one request, over https or http.
   - Redirects (301, 302, 303, 307, 308) are followed, and every hop is checked again, for its addresses and for the https rule, before it is requested. A redirect to another public https host fetches it (requests: original, then target) and stores the avatar. A redirect to a host resolving to 169.254.169.254, or to http on a foreign host, is never requested. A relative Location is resolved against the current URL ("/avatars/real.png" from https://cdn.example.com/users/1/a.png goes to https://cdn.example.com/avatars/real.png). At most MAX_PICTURE_REDIRECTS (3) redirects are followed, so a longer chain makes exactly 4 requests and then gives up. An empty Location counts as a redirect to the same URL and is followed up to that cap as well (4 requests).
   - The body is refused when Content-Length declares more than MAX_PICTURE_BYTES (5 MiB), or when more than that arrives while streaming, whatever Content-Length said.
   - On any refusal or failure (blocked address, an error status such as 404, a connection error such as httpx.ConnectError, a body too large, an undecodable image) the avatar is skipped: login still succeeds, external_avatar_hash stays null and cache_key does not change. On success, profile.webp appears in PrivateUser.get_directory(user_id), external_avatar_hash becomes the sha256 hex of the URL, cache_key changes, and the temporary image is moved into place with shutil.move as today (one move, nothing left at the source).
   - The rest of OIDC login (required claims, user and admin groups, default group and household, email verification, account adoption, claim logging) is unchanged.

UI changes (an in-app announcement about the new settings) are not part of this task.
